result.persona: ASHA community health worker doing door-to-door outreach in a rural Tamil Nadu panchayat, carrying a stack of paper registers and a low-end Android phone with patchy 4G. Tamil-first, limited English, self-taught on WhatsApp/YouTube, covering ~1,000 people and juggling TB, maternal, NCD, immunisation and survey duties on a sub-Rs 10,000 honorarium.
result.track: AI for Good Health & Well-being (SDG 3)

pains.title: I enter the same data twice — once on paper, then again in five apps that don't talk to each other
pains.description: Every household visit gets written into my paper register, then re-keyed into ANMOL, RCH Portal, Poshan Tracker, NIKSHAY and e-Sanjeevani — apps that are not interoperable, so the same pregnancy or child gets typed 4-5 times. Just the digital data-entry eats ~4 hours a day before I even walk to a single home. On a low-end phone with weak signal I also have to retry failed uploads and re-correct entries at night, sometimes asking my children to help. This is the single biggest daily time-thief and it means less time actually caring for people.
pains.whoAffected: Nearly all ~1 million ASHAs nationally and ~40,000+ in Tamil Nadu; worst for older, low-literacy workers on cheap phones
pains.currentGap: The government apps are siloed and were built top-down; nobody built a single Tamil-first capture layer that fans one input out to many forms, so redundancy is baked in and unremoved.
pains.evidence: ASHAs maintain 10+ registers plus digital input; ANMOL and RCH Portal are not interoperable; digital tasks alone take ~4 hours/day (New Lines Magazine 2025, 'India's Digital Health Push Is Overworking Its Front-Line Women'; datasyn.substack.com 'When Care Work Becomes Data Work')

pains.title: I miss danger signs in high-risk pregnancies and newborns because I have no decision support in the field
pains.description: When I sit with a pregnant woman or a 3-day-old baby, I have to judge from memory whether swelling, bleeding, fever, fast breathing or poor feeding is an emergency needing immediate referral. Studies show only about half of us can list all the danger signs, and anaemia/hypertension cues get missed. When I get it wrong a woman reaches the PHC or the Boyle/Janani van too late. This is the pain that actually costs lives, not just hours.
pains.whoAffected: Pregnant women, newborns and mothers in villages far from a functional CHC/FRU; every ASHA doing ANC/PNC home visits
pains.currentGap: Refresher training is one-size-fits-all, infrequent and in English; there is no offline, Tamil, symptom-in symptom-out triage aid in my hand at the doorstep.
pains.evidence: Only 49.5% of ASHAs identified all pregnancy danger signs; knowledge on anaemia and danger signs found inadequate; ASHAs often don't screen newborns for danger signs (Research Square 2025 Magadi Taluk study; BMC Pregnancy & Childbirth 2022 Rajasthan referral barriers)

pains.title: The apps are in English with layered menus, so I fight the tool instead of using it
pains.description: The forms use English medical terms and deep nested menus. I speak and read Tamil; I can manage WhatsApp and YouTube but not a 6-screen government form full of English labels. So I default back to paper, fall behind, or make wrong entries. A survey found 64% of rural women can't do basic smartphone tasks — the digital push assumes a literacy I and my peers don't have, and no amount of 'training' fixes an English-only interface.
pains.whoAffected: Low-literacy, Tamil-only ASHAs (a large share are older women from marginalised communities); rural women beneficiaries too
pains.currentGap: State health apps ship English-first with complex UIs; there is no conversational Tamil voice front-door that lets me just speak what I did and confirm it.
pains.evidence: 2025 govt survey: 64% of rural women cannot perform basic smartphone tasks; workers struggle with 'layered menus, English terminology and complex forms'; ASHAs demand language-specific training (New Lines Magazine 2025; ideasforindia.in on digitalisation double-edged sword)

pains.title: I chase my own incentive payments for months and never know why they're stuck
pains.description: My pay is per-activity incentives, but claims sit unpaid for two to three months (sometimes years), part-payments arrive with no explanation, and the ASHA-Nidhi portal shows irregularities I can't decode. I spend unpaid days at the PHC assembling proof of work I already did. The opacity — not knowing the status of my own money — is demoralising and is what drives the strikes.
pains.whoAffected: Every incentive-paid ASHA; acute where portal reconciliation fails and claims are documentation-heavy
pains.currentGap: Claim evidence is scattered across my registers and the very apps that don't talk to each other; there's no system that auto-assembles a claim from my logged activity or explains a rejection.
pains.evidence: Karnataka ASHAs owed Rs 5,000/month for 2-3 months up to 8 years; central Rs 7,000 incentives part-paid due to ASHA-Nidhi portal irregularities; 'status of payments remained unknown to all stakeholders' (Deccan Herald Jan 2025; Heinrich Boll Stiftung 2025 'Care Without Compensation')

pains.title: I lose track of who is due for follow-up across hundreds of households in a paper register
pains.description: For TB adherence, NCD (BP/sugar) recheck, ANC visit schedules and immunisation due-dates, I'm supposed to remember from a paper register who to visit which day across ~1,000 people. Defaulters slip through — a TB patient who stops drugs, a hypertensive who never returns for confirmation. Diagnosis turnaround is already slow, and without a prioritised daily worklist the sickest people quietly fall off my radar.
pains.whoAffected: TB, hypertension and diabetes patients; pregnant women and infants needing timely repeat contact
pains.currentGap: Follow-up scheduling lives in my head and on paper; existing apps record events but don't hand me a ranked 'who to see today' list in Tamil with reminders.
pains.evidence: 'Low turnaround for diagnosis confirmation a consistent issue'; multi-component tools needed to support ASHAs in referral/defaulter tracking (Nature Sci Reports 2025 ASHA-led diabetes mHealth; ScienceDirect 2024 NCD CHW training; NCD screening via ASHA under NHM)

result.persona: District Health Officer (DHO) accountable for PHC/HSC performance, drug stock, and maternal-child health metrics across a rural Tamil Nadu district — I answer to the Director of Public Health on dashboards I don't trust, with staff vacancies and paper-bound field workers.
result.track: AI for Good Health & Well-being (SDG 3)

pains.title: Drug stock-out blindness across my PHCs — I find out after patients are turned away
pains.description: I am accountable for essential-drug availability across dozens of PHCs and hundreds of sub-centres, but I only 'see' stock through monthly HMIS reports that are already stale by the time they reach me. Reorders are threshold/passbook based, not consumption-forecast based, so seasonal spikes (fever season, TB, insulin, iron-folic-acid) hit as stock-outs while other PHCs are sitting on soon-to-expire surplus 30km away. I have no live redistribution view. When a stock-out hits, patients get a handwritten chit to buy outside, the whole point of free public care collapses, and it lands on my desk as a complaint, not a forecast.
pains.whoAffected: DHO/DDHS, PHC pharmacists and medical officers, TNMSC warehouse staff, and ultimately rural patients (TB, maternal, diabetic, hypertensive) sent to buy drugs they can't afford
pains.currentGap: Tamil Nadu's TNMSC passbook system triggers reorders on static min-levels, not AI demand forecasting; the DHO sees consumption only in retrospective monthly HMIS, and there is no inter-PHC redistribution engine that matches near-expiry surplus at one facility to shortfall at another.
pains.evidence: During the 2024 nationwide TB-drug stockout, Tamil Nadu's stock lasted only ~10 days, forcing emergency local purchase (The Hindu/PressReader, Apr 2024); the 2025 Mudhalvar Marundhagam scheme launched with supply crunches, delayed supplies and only 300-400 of the intended generics stocked (The Federal, 2025).

pains.title: High-risk pregnancies and severe maternal anemia slip through until it's an emergency
pains.description: Maternal mortality is the metric I'm judged hardest on, yet my early-warning system is an ANM's handwritten ANC register. Anemia is rampant and it's the silent driver of postpartum haemorrhage deaths, but a Hb of 7 recorded in a register in a remote sub-centre doesn't automatically flag to me as a high-risk case needing IFA/IV-iron escalation or a planned institutional delivery with blood arranged. High-risk mothers who miss ANC visits or drop out just disappear from view until they arrive in obstetric crisis. I'm reacting to maternal near-misses instead of being warned weeks ahead.
pains.whoAffected: Pregnant women in rural blocks, ANMs and VHNs, PHC medical officers, the DHO owning district MMR and institutional-delivery targets
pains.currentGap: RCH-portal registration is incentivized but the DHO gets no automatic risk-stratification or dropout alert; identifying high-risk mothers (severe anemia, prior C-section, hypertension, missed visits) depends on an overloaded ANM manually flagging from paper — so cases surface late.
pains.evidence: NFHS-4 found 56.9% of reproductive-age women in Tamil Nadu anemic; rural pregnancy anemia runs ~54% nationally and anemia is a leading contributor to maternal mortality in India (PMC studies, incl. 2023-2025 reviews on maternal anemia and offspring outcomes).

pains.title: My field workers drown in duplicate registers, so the dashboards I'm judged on are garbage
pains.description: Every ANM and ASHA re-enters the same encounter into 10+ paper registers plus the RCH portal plus HMIS, often from memory at day's end, in Tamil, on a low-end phone with patchy signal. The result: data that is late, duplicated, and wrong. When my district dashboard says 92% ANC coverage, I genuinely don't know if that's real or register-filling before a review meeting. I make decisions and answer to the Director of Public Health on numbers I can't trust, and my staff spend their evenings on paperwork instead of home visits.
pains.whoAffected: ASHAs, ANMs, VHNs (the reporting burden), block medical officers, and the DHO whose every decision rests on this data quality
pains.currentGap: Registration/service data must be keyed into RCH portal and HMIS with penalties for incompleteness, but there is no Tamil voice-or-photo-to-structured-data capture that works offline on low-end Android; entry is manual, duplicated across registers, and unverified, so no downstream analytics can be trusted.
pains.evidence: RCH-portal completeness is tied to incentives/penalties and relies on manual data entry from sub-centre level (NHM RCH portal guidelines, 2024); Tamil Nadu HMIS is compiled from item-wise monthly manual district reports (data.gov.in OGD HMIS Tamil Nadu), i.e. retrospective and entry-dependent.

pains.title: NCD patients get screened once and then vanish — my screening numbers are theatre
pains.description: We screen huge volumes for hypertension and diabetes under Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam / NPCDCS, and I report big screening totals. But screening a person and controlling their disease are different worlds: once diagnosed, patients quietly stop refilling drugs, skip follow-up, and drift into strokes, renal failure and diabetic complications that flood my sub-district hospital. I have no prioritized 'who is about to drop out / who is uncontrolled' list — just a flat count of people screened. The care cascade leaks massively between screening and control and I can't see the leak, let alone plug it with targeted outreach.
pains.whoAffected: Rural hypertensive/diabetic adults, MTM/NCD nurses doing home delivery, PHC MOs, and the DHO reporting NCD control (not just screening) numbers
pains.currentGap: NPCDCS/CBAC captures screening, but there is no AI that flags likely-to-drop-out or uncontrolled patients from refill gaps and reading trends to drive prioritized outreach — follow-up depends on manual recall by overstretched staff.
pains.evidence: TN STEPS 2020 found 33.9% hypertension and 17.6% diabetes prevalence; a 2025 medRxiv care-cascade study explicitly targets the gap between screening and BP/sugar control, and rural TN medication-adherence studies (PMC, 2025) document poor adherence among diagnosed patients.

pains.title: Outbreaks announce themselves a week late — by then it's already a cluster
pains.description: Disease surveillance still reaches me as weekly IDSP tallies, so a fever/dengue/GI cluster in a village is often several days old before it's a 'signal' I can act on. My district lab capacity is thin, and the syndromic complaints that would tip me off early — a spike of fevers at one PHC, a WhatsApp rumour of diarrhoea in a hamlet — never get aggregated into an early-warning view. Every day of delay in detection is more cases, more panic, and a harder, costlier containment. I'm always one week behind the mosquito.
pains.whoAffected: Whole rural communities at outbreak risk, PHC MOs and health inspectors, district epidemiologist/RRT, and the DHO responsible for containment
pains.currentGap: IHIP/IDSP reporting is still effectively weekly and manual at the periphery, only ~13% of sanctioned IDSP district labs are functional, and there is no AI aggregating syndromic/OPD and community signals into real-time cluster alerts before lab confirmation.
pains.evidence: Roughly one-third of surveillance events in India are reported with delay and follow-up reports are often absent (IDSP 2018-2023 Lancet Regional Health SEA analysis, 2025); a 2026 dengue-surveillance case study found only ~13% of sanctioned IDSP district labs functional and outbreak reports published only weekly.

result.persona: Selvi, 38, runs a Mahalir Thittam self-help-group micro-enterprise in a village outside Coimbatore. I make banana-flour murukku, mango pickle, and millet snacks with 4 other women. I studied to 8th standard, speak Tamil, and share one low-end Android phone with my daughter. We sell at the Friday sandhai and to a broker who comes with a van. I want a bank loan to buy a sealing machine and to sell beyond my village, but every step assumes I read English forms, own a smartphone I understand, and have papers I do not have.
result.track: AI for Zero Hunger & Economic Growth (SDG 2 & 8)

pains.title: The broker sets my price and I have no number to argue back with
pains.description: The van-broker who buys our pickle and snacks dictates the rate — he knows I have no cold storage, no other buyer, and perishable stock that rots by Monday. I sell pickle at 90 rupees that reaches a Coimbatore shop shelf at 220. I have no idea what the 'real' rate is on any given week, so I cannot negotiate; I just take what he offers or watch the batch spoil. Direct-to-consumer sounds nice but I cannot reach those consumers.
pains.whoAffected: Rural SHG women producing pickles, snacks, millet foods, handicrafts who depend on weekly markets or a single aggregator/middleman
pains.currentGap: Mandi/market prices exist in scattered govt portals in English; there is no Tamil, voice-first tool that tells me a fair farm-gate/wholesale range for MY product this week and drafts a counter-offer. SHE-MART/eSaras are top-down platforms I am not onboarded to.
pains.evidence: ORF/Organiser (2026) and IUP Journal of Marketing Management (Feb 2025) both document SHG women 'depending on middlemen who dictate prices and profits,' with producers 'rarely receiving the full value of their work' — the explicit rationale for the Govt's 2026 SHE-MART initiative.

pains.title: I cannot get my products onto any digital market — the listing itself defeats me
pains.description: To sell on WhatsApp Business, ONDC, or a district portal I must write a product description in English, take clean photos, set categories, and often show a GST number. On a shared 2GB phone, in Tamil, with no one to help, I never finish. A one-time NGO camp listed our products once; the moment they left, nobody could add a new batch. So we fall back to the sandhai and the broker.
pains.whoAffected: First-time women digital sellers in SHGs with low literacy, shared low-end phones, no e-commerce experience
pains.currentGap: ONDC/marketplaces need catalog copy, clean product photos, categorisation and GST — a steep curve NGOs cross once then leave. No tool turns a spoken Tamil sentence + a phone snapshot into a ready listing that I can maintain myself.
pains.evidence: Nasscom Foundation–ONDC (2025) had to send staff on-ground for 'training, cataloguing and GST registration' for just 200 women; reports note 'hurdles in digitizing product catalogs, managing GST compliance' and a 'steep learning curve for first-time digital sellers.'

pains.title: Getting an enterprise loan means English forms, papers I don't have, and weeks of trips — so I go to the moneylender
pains.description: To buy a sealing machine I need maybe 40,000 rupees. The bank wants documents, a project plan, and repeated branch visits during my selling hours; officers say my SHG's paperwork is 'incomplete.' Each rejected trip costs a day's earnings and bus fare. When it drags on, I borrow from the local moneylender at brutal interest to not miss the season.
pains.whoAffected: SHG women seeking micro-enterprise (not just consumption) loans; those in remote areas with documentation gaps
pains.currentGap: Even with TNSRLM interest subvention and TN-RISE, the friction is credit-readiness: knowing which scheme fits, what documents, and drafting the application in Tamil. No AI assistant walks me through eligibility and pre-fills the paperwork.
pains.evidence: Academia/GAPGYAN (TN SHG studies, 2024-25) cite 'limited access to formal credit, documentation issues and bureaucratic hurdles' and 'inadequate financial literacy' as core barriers; TN launched TN-RISE/interest-subvention in 2024-25 specifically because credit + marketing access remain unsolved.

pains.title: The compliance maze — FSSAI licence, labelling, packaging — keeps my food business informal and unsellable to shops
pains.description: Any shop or online buyer asks for an FSSAI number, and packaged food must legally carry batch number, mfg/expiry date, ingredients, nutrition, and the FSSAI logo. I do not know which category I fall in, whether my turnover needs 'registration' or a full 'licence,' or how to make a compliant label. So I stay unbranded, unbanked-by-retail, and stuck at the weekly market.
pains.whoAffected: Women running home-kitchen / food-processing micro-enterprises (pickles, snacks, millet, spices)
pains.currentGap: FSSAI rules changed again in July 2024 (bold salt/sugar/fat labelling) and thresholds were revised; guidance is dense English/legal text. No Tamil, voice tool tells me 'you need X, here is your label, here is the form.'
pains.evidence: FSSAI Labelling & Display Regs 2020 + July 2024 amendment mandate batch no., dates, FSSAI logo/licence no. and bold nutrient labelling; Chambers/velcolegal (2024-26) note revised turnover thresholds meant to 'bring micro-enterprises into compliance' — but the burden of knowing/complying still falls on me.

pains.title: Our accounts live in a paper ledger that nobody can read back — and one error breaks group trust
pains.description: Our SHG savings, member loans, and repayments are in a hand-written notebook kept by whoever is bookkeeper. When entries are wrong or a page is lost, members fight over who repaid what, and the bank linkage stalls. At month-end nobody can quickly say our balance or who is overdue. I spend evenings reconciling instead of producing.
pains.whoAffected: SHG animators/bookkeepers and members managing group savings and internal loans
pains.currentGap: TNSRLM/Mahalir Thittam still train bookkeepers on manual registers (attendance, cash book, loan register, passbooks). A voice-driven Tamil ledger that logs 'Kamala paid 500 today,' flags overdue, and prints a bank-ready statement does not exist at group level.
pains.evidence: TN Mahalir Thittam (Pudukkottai/Ariyalur govt pages, current) still mandate manual Attendance & Resolution Book, Cash Book & Ledger, Saving & Loan register and member passbooks; World Bank Social Observatory notes bookkeeping-quality as a persistent SHG weak point (Mahakalasm MIS work).

result.persona: Informal settlement resident in a Tamil Nadu city (a tin/asbestos-roof hut in a Chennai or Coimbatore slum), a daily-wage earner and mother, Tamil-speaking, low-literate, using a shared low-end Android on patchy data. My days are wrecked by killing indoor heat, unreliable water, and a lane that floods and stinks every rain.
result.track: AI for Sustainable Cities & Climate Action (SDG 11 & 13)

pains.title: Killer indoor night heat with no warning that ever reaches me
pains.description: My asbestos/tin roof turns the hut into an oven. The urban heat island keeps my lane 3-7C hotter than the rest of the city at night, so my kids cannot sleep and the elderly collapse. The state's IMD 'moderate' warning and wet-bulb numbers never reach me in a form I understand, and I have no idea where the nearest cooling shelter, shaded spot, or free water point is. By the time anyone acts, someone is already sick.
pains.whoAffected: Slum families under tin/asbestos roofs, infants, the elderly, and outdoor daily-wage workers across Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai
pains.currentGap: Tamil Nadu declared heat a state disaster and has Heat Action Plans + a new Heat Resilience Centre, but experts flag a huge implementation gap: warnings are generic district-level English/technical alerts, not hyperlocal Tamil voice advice, and there is no map telling a slum resident which nearby shelter/water point/shade to reach right now.
pains.evidence: India's 2024 heatwave was its longest since 2010 with ~44,000 heatstroke cases; UHI keeps cities 3-7C hotter, turning an IMD 'moderate' alert into a public-health emergency for slum dwellers; Chennai children in informal settlements report sleepless nights (WRI India; scroll.in/eco-business; NCBI PMC8609203)

pains.title: Heat wipes out my daily wage and I get no advice on when/how to work safely
pains.description: I sell/labour outdoors. When wet-bulb temperature climbs my body cannot cope, but I cannot afford to stop. In 2025 nearly all vendors like me cut hours and lost most customers. Nobody tells me in advance which hours tomorrow are dangerous, when to shift my selling to early morning/evening, or that I am owed rest/relief. The current heat plans acknowledge my problem but do nothing that reaches my phone.
pains.whoAffected: Street vendors, construction and gig workers, waste-pickers, auto/loading workers in the urban informal economy
pains.currentGap: HAPs 'acknowledge the problem and do not solve it' for informal workers; there is no personalised, occupation-aware, Tamil-language heat-and-earnings advisory (best hours to work, when to rest, where to claim relief) delivered to a low-end phone.
pains.evidence: South Indian informal workers are 17x more likely to suffer heat productivity loss than formal workers; in the 2025 heatwave 90% of vendors cut hours and 96% reported a sharp fall in customers; every 1C rise in wet-bulb temp cut net earnings (Nature d44151-025-00193-0; Deccan Herald)

pains.title: Water never comes when I expect it, so I lose wages queuing or pay tankers I can't afford
pains.description: My lane has no reliable household pipeline. Supply is intermittent and unannounced, so I waste hours guarding pots or lose a work day, and in summer I pay ₹1,000+ a month to private tankers that barely deliver enough. When the tanker is late nobody tells me, and 70% of the water is contaminated so my family gets sick on top of it.
pains.whoAffected: Slum and low-income households on intermittent/tanker supply, especially women who bear the collection burden
pains.currentGap: Boards like CMWSSB run tankers and intermittent supply but give residents no predictable, Tamil, phone-accessible schedule or last-mile 'tanker is 20 min away / today's supply skipped' signal; municipalities assume slums 'need only a few gallons', so no household-level info service exists.
pains.evidence: Low-income households spend ₹500-1,000/month on private tankers; a resident paid ₹1,200 for a tanker that 'barely delivered enough' and borrowed money for water; 70% of TN water is contaminated; 13 districts incl. Chennai saw groundwater decline in May 2025 (thefinancialworld.com; thefederal.com; TN WRD May 2025)

pains.title: My lane floods and stays waterlogged every rain because the drain never worked here
pains.description: When it rains my low-lying settlement floods first and drains last. Stormwater 'completed' on paper but my area has missing drain links, silted catch-pits, and sewage that backs up into the water. I get no lane-level warning to move my things or my children before the water rises, and coastal high tide keeps us waterlogged for days even after light rain.
pains.whoAffected: Over 1 million Chennai informal-settlement residents in low-lying/coastal flood zones and similar pockets statewide
pains.currentGap: GCC claims 88% of stormwater drains done (₹6,475 cr, 1,235 km) yet residents report persistent yearly flooding from missing links and poor maintenance; there is no hyperlocal, lane-level flood early-warning + drainage-fault map that a resident can read/act on in Tamil.
pains.evidence: >1 million Chennai residents in informal settlements are highly flood-vulnerable; despite ₹6,475 cr on 1,235 km of drains residents flag missing SWD links, silted catch-pits and yearly flooding; coastal high-tide prolongs waterlogging (Citizen Matters pre-poll report; OpenCity Chennai Rains Datajam Jan 2024; SpiritOfChennai)

pains.title: Stagnant water and garbage breed dengue and my complaint goes nowhere until someone dies
pains.description: Open drains, sewage stagnation and dumped water-holding junk in my settlement breed Aedes mosquitoes; dengue and typhoid keep hitting my family. When I complain about a blocked drain or a breeding pool, response is slow — fogging and spraying only happen after cases or a death occur. I don't know how to file a complaint that actually gets tracked and escalated.
pains.whoAffected: Slum residents (esp. north Chennai) exposed to open drains, sewage stagnation and waste-driven mosquito breeding
pains.currentGap: Grievance flow is slow and reactive; there is no easy way to photograph a breeding site/blocked drain, auto-classify severity, auto-file a tracked complaint in Tamil, and escalate before an outbreak — action currently comes only after cases/deaths.
pains.evidence: TN logged 27,378 dengue cases + 13 deaths in 2024 and 16,546 in 2025 (India's 2nd-highest); officials blame stagnant water; Chennai residents blame officials for water stagnation/garbage and say action comes only after cases/deaths; 20,455 kg of water-holding containers cleared in June alone (medindia.net; dtnext.in; newkerala.com)

result.persona: District Environmental Engineer, Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board (TNPCB) — one officer responsible for an entire district's air, water, and industrial pollution enforcement, with a handful of field staff and a fistful of sensors.
result.track: AI for Sustainable Cities & Climate Action (SDG 11 & 13)

pains.title: I am blind everywhere except a few city intersections
pains.description: My real-time monitoring network is a joke against the geography I'm accountable for. Tamil Nadu's continuous air-quality stations (CAAQMS) are clustered in Chennai, Coimbatore, Trichy, Madurai and a handful of industrial towns — Chennai alone is judged to need 20 stations but has ~8. My rural blocks, brick kilns, quarries, and small dyeing clusters have ZERO real-time eyes. When the boss or the NGT asks 'what's the air/water quality in taluk X right now,' I have a manual sample I took two weeks ago and a lab report that's still pending. I physically cannot be in 15 places at once, so 90% of my district is an unmonitored blind spot and I only find out about a problem after someone falls sick or a river runs black.
pains.whoAffected: District environmental engineers + their 3-4 field staff; the lakhs of rural residents living downstream/downwind of unmonitored sources
pains.currentGap: CAAQMS cost ~Rs 1-1.5 crore each and are politically placed in cities; there is no system that fuses the sparse official sensors with satellite data + weather to ESTIMATE pollution where no sensor exists and tell me where to drive tomorrow. Plain dashboards just replot the same 8 dots.
pains.evidence: TNPCB runs CAAQMS concentrated in Chennai (~8), Coimbatore (3), Trichy (5), Madurai (3) etc.; Chennai alone 'needs at least 20 stations' (Citizen Matters, 2024). India's rural network was only 26 stations across 26 villages nationwide as of Nov 2024 (CPCB). Grew from 3 to 8 in Chennai since 2019 — still a fraction of need.

pains.title: Complaints drown me and I can't tell the emergency from the noise
pains.description: My phone, the OLGPRS complaint portal, WhatsApp, and the Collector's office all funnel pollution complaints at me — mostly voice notes and blurry photos in Tamil: 'stench near our street', 'foam in the canal', 'they're burning something at night'. There is no triage. A genuinely dangerous chromium discharge sits in the same undifferentiated pile as a neighbour dispute about a generator. I read them one by one, half are duplicates of the same event, half have no usable location, and by the time I dispatch someone the polluter has stopped. Citizens conclude TNPCB does nothing, and honestly from their side it looks that way.
pains.whoAffected: Me and my field team; every citizen who reports and hears nothing back; TNPCB's credibility
pains.currentGap: The existing OLGPRS complaint register is a dumb form — no NLP on Tamil text/voice, no auto-geolocation from photos, no de-duplication, no severity ranking, no clustering of many reports into one incident. Triage is fully manual on an already overloaded officer.
pains.evidence: TNPCB's public grievance is the OLGPRS 'Complaint Register' portal (tnpcb.gov.in/olgprs) — a plain form with no intelligence. SPCBs run with >50% of sanctioned posts vacant (6,075 of 12,016 unfilled, NGT report via Mongabay 2022; CPR 2022 'human resource crunch'), so triage labor simply doesn't exist.

pains.title: Factories dump at night, exactly when no inspector is watching
pains.description: The tanneries around Vellore/Vaniyambadi and dyeing/bleaching units around Tirupur know my inspection hours. They run effluent treatment for the daytime visit and bypass it into the Palar or a storm drain after dark or during rain. I catch a fraction, and even then the effluent has moved downstream by the time my sample reaches the lab. Groundwater in these belts is already poisoned with chromium 5x the limit — the damage is irreversible and I'm always arriving after the fact, holding a violation notice for something I can't prove happened at 2am.
pains.whoAffected: Communities drinking contaminated groundwater in Vellore, Tirupur, Erode, Karur, Cuddalore, Manali; farmers with ruined land; me, holding legal liability I can't enforce
pains.currentGap: Continuous emission/effluent monitors (OCEMS) get tampered/bypassed and I have no analytics flagging suspicious dips; nothing cross-references satellite water-colour anomalies + rainfall + complaint clusters to PREDICT which unit is likely bypassing tonight so I inspect the right gate.
pains.evidence: Supreme Court (Jan 2025) held Vellore tanneries liable for 'irreversible damage' to the Palar via untreated effluent; ~240 tanneries discharge ~20 million litres/day, much untreated (Dialogue Earth). Vaniyambadi 2024 study: 140/140 groundwater samples exceeded thresholds, chromium 5x limit (India Water Portal, 2025). Vellore, Tirupur, Manali flagged CEPI 'critically polluted'.

pains.title: Open and waste burning happens at night across the district and I never see it
pains.description: Municipal solid waste, agricultural residue, plastic and tyres get openly burned across my rural blocks and at dumpyards — TNPCB itself lists open MSW and agri-residue burning as a top air-pollution source in places like Thoothukudi. It's dispersed, it's mostly after sunset, and I have no way to know it's happening until the PM spikes or a village complains of smoke. I can't attribute it, can't prove who lit it, and can't dispatch in time. It's a huge invisible chunk of my district's emissions and health load that never enters any of my records.
pains.whoAffected: Rural residents (respiratory harm from PM2.5 with toxic heavy metals); Thoothukudi & other non-attainment towns; me, blamed for AQI I can't source
pains.currentGap: NASA FIRMS/VIIRS satellite fire detections (375m) exist as raw open data but no local tool ingests them, filters to my jurisdiction, overlays wind trajectory to attribute a smoke plume to a location, and pushes me a same-night alert with a map pin.
pains.evidence: Study near Neyveli (TN): heavy metals in PM2.5 traced to open waste burning, 'more than coal' (Nature, 2025). TNPCB names MSW + agri-residue open burning among main sources in Thoothukudi, a CPCB non-attainment city (failed PM10 for 5 straight years). VIIRS S-NPP active-fire 375m data is public.

pains.title: When the heat kills, I have no map of who's about to die
pains.description: Tamil Nadu declared heatwave a state-specific disaster in Oct 2024 after 40C+ summers, promising Rs 4 lakh relief per death — which means the state now cares about heat, and that pressure lands partly on environmental/planning staff. But at the district and ULB level we have no fine-grained map of WHERE the danger concentrates: which slum wards, which bus stands, which outdoor-labour zones, which heat-island streets with no tree cover. The Heat Action Plan is a generic PDF. I'm asked to help target shelters, water points and work-hour changes, but I'm working off district-average temperature, not the block-level vulnerability that decides who actually collapses.
pains.whoAffected: Outdoor labourers, slum residents, elderly in un-treed heat-island wards; ULB and disaster-management officers who must place limited relief resources
pains.currentGap: Heat Action Plans are static documents; there's no tool fusing satellite land-surface-temperature + built-up density + tree cover + population vulnerability into a ward-level heat-risk map with a short-term forecast to pre-position relief. Current planning is district-average and reactive.
pains.evidence: TN notified heatwave as 'state disaster' (GO, Oct 2024) with Rs 4 lakh relief per victim; 13 heat deaths recorded 2023; April-May 2024 many regions >40C (dtnext; TN State Planning Commission 'Heat Mitigation Strategy'). Heat Action Plan is a general guideline PDF, not spatially targeted.

result.persona: Personal Assistant / office manager in a rural Tamil Nadu MP-cum-MLA constituency office — the person who actually runs the daily "grievance camp", logs public petitions, and prepares the MPLADS/CDF work recommendations the boss signs off to the District Collector. Overworked, 3-4 staff, everything on paper registers and WhatsApp, judged politically on "did our people's problems get solved and did our funds reach the ground before the next election."
result.track: AI for Strong Institutions (SDG 16)

pains.title: Our MPLADS/CDF money quietly lapses while I'm flying blind on where it should go
pains.description: Each MP gets Rs 5 crore/year to recommend works, but I have no consolidated view of what's already sanctioned, what's half-done, or which panchayats have been starved. Demands pile in from party workers and villages on scraps of paper; I can't tell duplicates from genuine gaps or match them to the unspent balance sitting with the Collector. Result: funds lapse, the opposition screams 'they didn't spend a rupee', and I find out too late.
pains.whoAffected: MP/MLA office staff, the elected member's political standing, and every village whose road/borewell never got funded because the money sat idle
pains.currentGap: MPLADS portal data is scattered across DM offices, in English, not linked to live constituency demand; prioritisation is done from memory and pressure, not need. No tool ties 'unspent balance' to 'ranked list of pending genuine demands'.
pains.evidence: MoSPI data: ~75% of MPLADS funds allotted to Tamil Nadu's 39 MPs (2019-24) went unutilised; works incomplete in 23 districts incl. Coimbatore, Pollachi, Tiruppur; A. Raja (Nilgiris) spent only ~3% (Rs 37L of Rs 9.8cr). Nationally Rs 1,729 cr unspent, ~53% utilisation (The Commune/MoSPI; factly.in; empoweredindian.in).

pains.title: Hundreds of Tamil handwritten petitions a week, and no way to track, dedupe or follow up
pains.description: At every weekly grievance camp people hand me petitions — handwritten Tamil, or dictated because they can't write. I log them in a register, forward some, and the rest vanish into a drawer. Same complaint comes 4 times from 4 villagers; a real emergency looks identical to a routine request. When the boss asks 'what happened to that widow's pension case', I have no answer. Voters conclude the office does nothing.
pains.whoAffected: Constituents (especially non-literate, elderly, women), the office's reputation, and me — I take the blame for every dropped case
pains.currentGap: Everything is paper/WhatsApp. No Tamil-first intake that turns a photo of a petition or a voice note into a structured, deduplicated, categorised, trackable case with a follow-up reminder. Govt portals are English-first and not built for camp-scale intake.
pains.evidence: TN runs paper/portal grievance systems (district Petition Processing Portal, CPGRAMS) with a 21-day norm; CPGRAMS handled 70+ lakh grievances 2022-24, and DARPG/PM flagged 'quality of disposal' as the core weakness — i.e. logging exists, tracking-to-resolution doesn't (DARPG CPGRAMS monthly reports 2024; pgportal.gov.in).

pains.title: I can't tell if a 'completed' work actually exists on the ground
pains.description: A work is marked in-progress or completed on paper by the contractor/engineer, but I have no independent proof the borewell was dug or the community hall built. When a villager complains 'nothing happened here', I'm stuck between the file and the field. Fake or padded completion certificates make our office look complicit, and CAG picks it apart later.
pains.whoAffected: The elected member (audit and reputational exposure), honest contractors, and villages that paid politically for phantom assets
pains.currentGap: No lightweight geo-tagged, photo-evidence verification loop tied to each sanctioned work; verification depends on trusting the same officials being audited. AI image checks (is this actually a road/borewell, does location match) aren't in the workflow.
pains.evidence: CAG and MoSPI data show works 'incomplete' across 23 TN districts despite fund release; MPLADS audits repeatedly flag incomplete/unverified assets and low utilisation (CAG TN Reports 2024, cag.gov.in; MoSPI performance report on mplads.gov.in).

pains.title: Once I forward a grievance to a line department, it disappears into a black hole
pains.description: Most cases aren't ours to fix directly — they go to Revenue, TANGEDCO, Health, Highways. I forward a letter and then have zero visibility. The department marks it 'resolved' without doing anything, the citizen re-petitions us angrier, and I re-forward the same thing. There's no closure loop I control, so the office absorbs the anger for another department's inaction.
pains.whoAffected: Citizens bounced between offices, MP/MLA office credibility, and inter-department accountability
pains.currentGap: No system that tracks a referred case to actual outcome, flags suspicious 'resolved-without-action' closures, and auto-escalates aged cases. CPGRAMS closures are known to be low-quality but the office has no independent check.
pains.evidence: DARPG itself made 'quality of disposal' the headline problem in 2024 CPGRAMS reviews; appeal facility exists precisely because citizens rate resolutions 'poor' and reopen — evidence that 'resolved' often isn't (DARPG 2024 CPGRAMS monthly reports; pgportal.gov.in appeal mechanism).

pains.title: At election time I can't produce a credible record of what we actually delivered
pains.description: The boss needs to prove 'we built X, solved Y grievances, spent Z crore where'. But our proof is fragmented registers, WhatsApp photos and memory. RTI activists and rivals compile our unspent-fund numbers faster than we can compile our achievements. Without a clean, evidence-backed delivery record, good work is politically invisible and easy to attack.
pains.whoAffected: The elected member's re-election case, office staff scrambling to reconstruct history, and voters trying to judge performance honestly
pains.currentGap: No system that continuously assembles sanctioned-vs-completed works, grievance stats and geotagged proof into a shareable, defensible constituency report. It's rebuilt by hand each time, always incomplete.
pains.evidence: Third parties already publish MP-wise MPLADS scorecards (empoweredindian.in MPLADS dashboard; factly.in) showing the 75% TN under-utilisation narrative — the office has no equivalent tool to tell its own verified side.

result.persona: Ramasamy, 68, a marginal farmer in a village near Pollachi (Coimbatore district). Has type 2 diabetes and high BP for 9 years, and last year the PHC put me on 6-month TB tablets too. I speak only Tamil, read very little, and use my son's old Android phone (WhatsApp and calls only). The nearest PHC is 14 km; the taluk hospital is 30 km. Every clinic visit costs me a day's wage and 100-150 rupees in bus/share-auto fare. I take five or six tablets a day and honestly I lose track of which is which.
result.track: AI for Good Health & Well-being (SDG 3)

pains.title: Six tablets a day, and I mix them up or forget half of them
pains.description: I take metformin, a BP tablet, sometimes two, plus the TB course. They are white and round and look the same to my eyes. Some are before food, some after, some at night. My wife reminds me but she forgets too. Half the days I skip one or double another. Nobody at home can read the strip to check. When my sugar or BP goes bad the doctor scolds me for 'not taking medicines properly' but the problem is I genuinely cannot keep the schedule straight in my head.
pains.whoAffected: Elderly rural patients on polypharmacy for chronic NCDs (diabetes, hypertension) and long-course TB; often low-literacy, managing 4-6 pills with different timing/food rules.
pains.currentGap: Paper leaflets and pill strips are in English/clinical terms; smartphone reminder apps assume literacy, app stores, and reading. No tool ties a specific pill photo to a plain-Tamil voice reminder that works on a basic phone offline.
pains.evidence: Rural Tamil Nadu (Tiruvallur) cross-sectional study, Cureus Aug 2025: only 58.5% medication adherence — nearly half non-adherent — with age and complexity of the drug regimen the significant predictors of poor adherence (PMC12381594). A 2024 India elderly study found low health literacy linked to 2.6x higher unintentional non-adherence.

pains.title: I cannot read my own prescription or lab report
pains.description: The doctor writes fast in English, hands me a slip, and the pharmacist mumbles. My blood report is a page of numbers I do not understand — is my sugar dangerous or fine? I nod like I understood and go home confused. When I mix up a dose it is often because I never understood the instruction in the first place. There is nobody in the village to sit and explain it in Tamil, and I am ashamed to keep asking.
pains.whoAffected: Low-literacy elderly and their family caregivers who receive prescriptions, discharge slips and lab reports in English/medical shorthand they cannot decode.
pains.currentGap: No accessible way to turn a photographed prescription or lab report into a spoken plain-Tamil explanation ('this tablet is for BP, one after breakfast; your sugar is high, cut rice'). Human explanation depends on an overloaded PHC or a literate relative who may not be around.
pains.evidence: 2024 India elderly readability study: only 37% could clearly read prescription label instructions (63% had difficulty), and just 8% said they 'always' understood them, with misunderstanding rising with age and lower education (RSIS/IJRISS 2024). Multimodal AI (photo to Tamil voice) is a strong fit vs plain software.

pains.title: The clinic is too far, so I only go when I am already sick
pains.description: A refill or a routine BP check means a full day gone: 14 km each way, waiting half the day, losing wages, and my knees cannot take the bus. So I stretch my tablets, skip follow-ups, and only make the trip when something is really wrong — by then my sugar is 300 or my feet are swollen. Many of us just quietly drop out of regular care because the distance is not worth it for 'feeling okay'.
pains.whoAffected: Elderly and poor rural NCD/TB patients living 10-30 km from a PHC/taluk hospital with no easy transport, for whom routine follow-up competes with a day's wage.
pains.currentGap: Follow-up is all-or-nothing: either travel in person or nothing. No trusted remote check-in that safely tells a patient 'your reported readings are fine, skip the trip' vs 'come in now', so people default to skipping and present late.
pains.evidence: Lancet/ScienceDirect 2024 study of elderly hypertension in rural India: 73% kept outpatient appointments when a clinic was within 10 km, but only 17% attended when the round trip was 11-30 km; ~10% of Indian villages are 10+ km from a PHC (S0277953624010670; medRxiv geospatial access 2025).

pains.title: Between visits I have no idea if my BP/sugar reading is dangerous
pains.description: Sometimes a health camp or the ASHA checks my BP or sugar and gives me a number. But then what? I go home with the number and no meaning. Is 180 by 100 an emergency or normal for an old man? My chest feels tight at night — do I wait till morning or rush 30 km in the dark? Without anyone to ask, I usually just wait, and waiting is what kills people like me.
pains.whoAffected: Chronic patients self-monitoring or getting camp/ASHA readings between clinic visits, plus family who must decide when a symptom is a red flag worth an emergency trip.
pains.currentGap: Readings and symptoms are captured but not interpreted at the patient's side. No Tamil, voice-first triage that turns 'BP 180/100 + chest tightness' into a clear 'go now' / 'okay, recheck tomorrow' with escalation to the PHC/ASHA.
pains.evidence: National Medical Journal of India: weak NCD follow-up and interpretation at rural primary-care level drives poor chronic-disease control; delayed presentation worsens outcomes (nmji.in NCD rural review). Distance-driven late presentation compounds it (Lancet elderly access study 2024).

pains.title: The TB tablets make me feel worse, so I want to quit halfway
pains.description: The 6-month TB course makes me nauseous, tired, and turns my urine orange — I feel sicker on the medicine than off it. Once I start feeling a little better after two months I think 'enough, I am cured' and want to stop. Nobody explains that stopping is dangerous, and the DOTS worker only sees me sometimes. Half the men in my situation just quietly stop and end up back in hospital worse than before.
pains.whoAffected: Rural TB (and other long-course) patients battling side effects, stigma and 'I feel fine now' beliefs during months-long treatment, often with thin frontline follow-up.
pains.currentGap: Ni-kshay tracks patients for the system, not for the patient — there is no patient-facing companion in Tamil to reassure about side effects, counter 'I'm cured' beliefs, and nudge daily doses, and ASHA/DOTS workers are too overloaded to call everyone daily.
pains.evidence: India TB Report 2024: loss-to-follow-up remains a top driver of persistent TB, with drug side effects, weak provider support, financial strain and stigma cited; nearly half of LTFU patients are rural (theanalysis.org.in India TB 2024; PLOS One LTFU studies). ASHAs are doing double paper+digital entry and report exhaustion, limiting per-patient follow-up (New Lines Magazine 2024).

result.persona: FPO manager / farmgate trader in a Tamil Nadu district — I aggregate produce from 300-800 smallholder members, negotiate with mandi commission agents and processors, arrange transport, and settle payments to farmers. My days are ruled by perishable stock, volatile prices, and paperwork.
result.track: AI for Zero Hunger & Economic Growth (SDG 2 & 8)

pains.title: Distress sale on harvest day — no forward price signal, so a glut wipes out the season
pains.description: When everyone in the region harvests the same crop the same week, the mandi floods and the farmgate price collapses below my members' cost of production. I have no reliable warning that a glut is coming, and my perishable stock cannot wait, so I dump it at whatever the commission agent offers or leave it to rot. My members then refuse to route future produce through the FPO because they blame me for the low realisation.
pains.whoAffected: FPO manager and 300-800 member smallholders; farmgate traders holding perishables like tomato, mango, banana, chilli
pains.currentGap: eNAM and mandi price boards only show TODAY's arrivals after the crash has already happened. There is no district-level, crop-level early warning that combines sowing/harvest timing across villages to predict oversupply days, and nothing in Tamil that a manager can act on 1-2 weeks ahead to stagger harvest or divert to processors.
pains.evidence: Melur (Madurai) mango farmgate price crashed to Rs 3/kg in 2024, forcing farmers to let 'Kili Mooku' rot or cut plantations; tomato prices fell 60-85% in TN/Karnataka gluts. Source: newkerala.com 'Mango Farmers in Madurai in Crisis' 2024; Deccan Herald tomato price crash 2024.

pains.title: No fast, trusted quality grading — buyers discount or reject my lots and I can't prove otherwise
pains.description: Buyers pay premium only for graded produce, but I have no quick assaying facility. Grading is done by the commission agent's eye, always in the buyer's favour, and I have no objective record to argue with. So mixed, ungraded lots get a blanket low price, and processors/exporters who want a specific grade won't even engage with my FPO because they don't trust my quality claims.
pains.whoAffected: FPO manager negotiating with processors, exporters, retail chains; members whose good produce is priced like their worst
pains.currentGap: Quick assaying/grading labs are absent at most mandis, so eNAM distant-buyer participation never picks up. Manual grading is subjective, slow, and disputable; there is no cheap way to grade a truckload on the spot and generate a shareable quality certificate a buyer will accept.
pains.evidence: Govt/research note eNAM stalled because 'lack of quick assaying facilities' blocks distant-trader participation and there is 'no standardised quality assessment of produce'. Post-harvest losses: tomato 11.6%, fruits up to 15%. Source: ACS Publisher IJEE eNAM TN adoption study; DownToEarth 'As told to Parliament' Aug 6 2024.

pains.title: Price information asymmetry — I don't know what my crop fetches in the next district, so the middleman does
pains.description: I only know my local mandi's rate. The commission agent knows prices in Chennai, Bengaluru, and Kochi and pockets the spread. Checking 5-6 mandis means 5-6 phone calls to people who lie to me. My members are Tamil-speaking with low-end phones and can't read the English/number-heavy eNAM portal, so real price discovery never reaches the farmgate.
pains.whoAffected: FPO manager and members deciding where and when to sell; anyone without a trader network
pains.currentGap: eNAM data is fragmented, English-heavy, requires literacy and internet, and shows raw arrivals not an actionable 'sell here vs there after transport cost' answer. No Tamil voice interface aggregates scattered mandi/eNAM feeds into a simple net-realisation comparison a farmer can trust.
pains.evidence: Research: 'farmers had no visibility into prices in distant markets, middlemen controlled the supply chain'; eNAM adoption constrained by 'low digital literacy, poor rural internet, entrenched middlemen'. Source: Amrita/eNAM case; ACS Publisher IJEE Tamil Nadu eNAM constraints study 2024.

pains.title: Can't reliably match my aggregated stock to a buyer who wants that grade and quantity now
pains.description: Aggregating 40 farmers' produce is only half the job — I then have to find a buyer who wants exactly this crop, grade, and volume within the 2-3 days before it spoils. Processors and bulk buyers hesitate to deal directly with FPOs, so I fall back on the same commission agent. Deals happen over scattered WhatsApp and phone calls with no way to broadcast 'I have 8 tonnes Grade-A tomato in Dharmapuri today'.
pains.whoAffected: FPO manager doing market linkage; institutional buyers, processors, quick-commerce and retail sourcing teams
pains.currentGap: Market-arrival/demand coordination platforms barely exist; buyers and FPOs discover each other ad hoc. No real-time lightweight board that matches a signalled lot (crop+grade+volume+location+ready-date) to standing buyer demand and handles the language gap.
pains.evidence: Field studies: 'major processors and output purchasing companies hesitate to engage directly with FPOs'; smallholders lack real-time harvest-readiness vs demand signalling. Source: StarAgri 'How FPOs Can Use AgriTech'; MicroSave 'Decoding agriculture market linkages for FPOs' 2023.

pains.title: Transport is unbooked and mistimed, so produce spoils or arrives when the market is already saturated
pains.description: I have no reliable way to book a vehicle or know when one is free, so I make rushed, half-empty trips that reach the mandi too early or too late. Small lots travel alone instead of pooling, transport cost per kg is brutal, and every hour of delay in the July heat is spoilage I eat. This is a direct chunk of my 5-15% post-harvest loss.
pains.whoAffected: FPO manager coordinating dispatch; members whose share shrinks with spoilage and freight cost
pains.currentGap: Smallholders have 'no reliable way to book transport or know when vehicles are available,' forcing unoptimised trips. No load-pooling/scheduling tool that combines multiple villages' lots into shared trips timed to market demand and cold-chain availability.
pains.evidence: Perishable-logistics analysis: no reliable transport booking causes 'rushed, unoptimized trips'; India loses 5-15% of fruits & vegetables post-harvest. Source: itln.in 'Demand up, but can India's perishable logistics deliver?'; DownToEarth Aug 6 2024 Parliament reply.

pains.title: Paper-bound member ledgers and delayed payments erode member trust and my working capital
pains.description: I settle hundreds of member payments off paper slips and a notebook — who delivered how much, at what grade, minus advances and transport. Reconciliation is slow and error-prone, payments to farmers lag by days or weeks, and one disputed entry breaks trust for the whole village. Meanwhile GST/compliance and buyer-payment delays choke my working capital and I have no clean records to show a lender for credit.
pains.whoAffected: FPO manager/board doing settlements and compliance; members waiting on payment; lenders assessing the FPO
pains.currentGap: Most FPOs run on paper and cannot access institutional credit partly for lack of clean books. No Tamil, voice/photo-first bookkeeping that turns delivery slips and weighbridge notes into member ledgers, auto-computes settlements, and produces lender-ready records.
pains.evidence: Springer 2025 study on TN farmer producer companies: 'lack of access to institutional credit' is the top constraint alongside 'payment delays'; management/record capacity is weak. Source: Springer Discover Sustainability 2025 'Financial health of farmer producer companies in Tamil Nadu'; ETV Bharat 'What Ails FPOs' 2024.

result.persona: Kavitha, 38, a farm labourer in a village near Tiruppur, Tamil Nadu. I have a low-end Android phone with patchy data. I need a community certificate for my daughter's college scholarship and I want the widow/old-age pension for my mother — but every counter, portal and form speaks a language of documents and rules I can't decode, and I lose days of daily wages each time I travel to the taluk office.
result.track: AI for Strong Institutions (SDG 16)

pains.title: My certificate gets rejected and nobody tells me WHY in words I understand
pains.description: I applied for my daughter's community certificate on e-Sevai. Weeks later the status just says 'Rejected'. The one-line reason is in bureaucratic English/technical Tamil about a 'document mismatch' or 'VAO remarks' I cannot parse. I don't know which of the 6 documents was wrong, or whether to fix the parents' certificate, the ration card, or the residence proof. So I travel back to the CSC operator (another lost wage day) who guesses, I reapply, and it bounces again. The reapply-guess-reject loop can run 3-4 times over two months.
pains.whoAffected: Rural applicants for community/income/nativity certificates who go through CSC operators or the portal; the poorest, least literate applicants get stuck in the loop longest because they can't self-diagnose the reason.
